## Installing the build toolchain

### Installing ARM GNU Toolchain

The [Arm GNU Toolchain][arm_gnu_toolchain] is the GNU cross-compiler toolchain
for Arm targets.

To download the cross-compiler, visit the website and scroll down to the list of
releases. Click on the link for the release you want and expand the collapsible
section for your host operating system (e.g. Windows, Linux, macOS). In the list
of toolchains, choose the download for a `arm-none-eabi` target.

> [!note] For Windows and macOS users
> You will have the option of downloading the cross-compiler toolchain in the
> form of an installer (i.e. `.msi` for Windows, `.pkg` for macOS). If you
> choose to use the installer, you must take note of the path where toolchain files
> are installed. For Windows, the installer will show the path during installation.
> For macOS, you will have to search for the files, although they likely will appear
> under `/Applications/`.

If you are not using the installer, download the archive for the toolchain and
extract it to a known location. For example, under a `/projects/devkits/` folder.

For both an installer and archive, you will have to add the toolchain binaries
to your system path so that you can run it from the command line. In the extracted
directory of your toolchain, you will see a `bin/` folder. This `bin/` folder
must contain files named `arm-none-eabi-*` (e.g. `arm-none-eabi-gdb`). **If you
do not see these files, you are in the wrong folder!** Go up 2 directory levels
and look for the `bin/` folder again. Take the full path of the `bin/` folder
and add it to your system path. How you set this will depend on your operating
system, so consult online resources!

To verify you have installed the toolchain correctly, run the command for
your operating system in a new terminal (ensure your current working directory
is NOT in the `bin/` folder).

```shell
# Windows
arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe --version

# macOS
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version

# Linux
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
```

You should see an output that looks like the following if it is installed correctly.

```
arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arm GNU Toolchain 15.3.Rel1 (Build arm-15.149)) 15.3.1 20260627
Copyright (C) 2025 Free Software Foundation, Inc.
This is free software; see the source for copying conditions.  There is NO
warranty; not even for MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.
```

[arm_gnu_toolchain]: https://developer.arm.com/downloads/-/arm-gnu-toolchain-downloads

### Installing Ninja

[Ninja][ninja_build] is the build system we use for the firmware. You will not
interact with it directly, but rather through CMake.

It can be installed by following the steps on the site.

You can verify your installation by running the command

```shell
ninja --version
```

[ninja_build]: https://ninja-build.org

### Installing CMake

[CMake][cmake] is the meta-build system that we use for the firmware.

Follow the instructions on its site to download and install it for your host
machine. Ensure that you are using a version greater or equal to `3.22`.

You can verify your installation by running the command

```shell
cmake --version
```

[cmake]: https://cmake.org

## Setting up VS Code

We use [Visual Studio Code (VS Code)][vscode] as our primary development editor.

[vscode]: https://code.visualstudio.com

### Installing VS Code

Follow the steps provided by the official guide on
[Setting up Visual Studio Code][setting_up_vscode].

[setting_up_vscode]: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/setup-overview

### Installing recommended extensions

> [!important]
> Unless you have your own working extension setup, you should definitely
> install these recommended extensions.

To view the recommended extensions, open the VS Code Command Palette
(`Ctrl+Shift+P` or `Cmd+Shift+P`) and run the
`Extensions: Show Recommended Extensions` command. This will open up the
`WORKSPACE RECOMMENDATIONS` section of the `EXTENSIONS` sidebar. To download all
the recommended extensions, click the `Install Workspace Recommended Extensions`
button (displayed as a cloud icon).

Alternatively, you can install the recommended extensions manually using the
extension identifiers listed in `.vscode/extensions.json`.

## Adding debugging support to VS Code

This section will describe how to setup remote debugging support in VS Code for
the firmware.

### Installing pyOCD

pyOCD is a Python command line tool that provides a bunch of debugging functionality
for Arm Cortex MCUs. It is similar to tools like OpenOCD and J-Link.

Importantly for us, it provides a GDB server that allows us to debug the MCU over a
console or GUI debugger.

pyOCD provides an [official install guide][pyocd_install_guide] that you should follow.
It officially lists `pip` and `pipx` as the package installer you should use for the 
tool. However, I would also recommend you consider package managers like [uv][uv_package_manager].
If you are using `uv`, you can install pyOCD using the command

```shell
uv install tool pyocd
```

To verify that you installed pyOCD correctly, run the following command

```shell
pyocd --version
```

[pyocd_install_guide]: https://pyocd.io/docs/installing.html
[uv_package_manager]: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/

### Fixing pyOCD USB permissions for Linux

> [!note] This section is for Linux users only
> If you are not a Linux user, you can ignore this section.

As a rule of thumb, **do not run pyOCD with sudo privileges**.

Follow the official pyOCD installation guide for setting up udev rules.
They have provided an official set of rules that you can use to get support
for your specific debug probe.

### Adding MCU support to pyOCD

For detailed information about pyOCD support for various targets, see the official
[target support documentation][pyocd_target_support].

pyOCD has builtin support for a set of MCUs. You can list all the supported builtin
targets using

```shell
pyocd list --targets -s builtin
```

If you don't see your MCU listed, you can add support for it through CMSIS Device
Family Packs (DFP). To install a DFP for your MCU, first try searching for the
exact DFP name using

```shell
pyocd pack find <family>
```

For example, for a `STM32H745ZIT6` MCU, you can use the command

```shell
pyocd pack find STM32H745Z
```

and receive the following list

```shell
  Part            Vendor               Pack                 Version   Installed  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  STM32H745ZGTx   STMicroelectronics   Keil.STM32H7xx_DFP   4.1.3     True       
  STM32H745ZITx   STMicroelectronics   Keil.STM32H7xx_DFP   4.1.3     True       
```

then you can install the DFP using the part name `STM32H745ZITx`

```shell
pyocd pack install STM32H745ZITx
```

If you have installed the DFP correctly, running

```shell
pyocd list --targets
```

should show the MCU you wanted to add (i.e. `STM32H745ZITx`).

[pyocd_target_support]: https://pyocd.io/docs/target_support.html

## Optional tools

These are tools that are not used regularly for development but may have
a purpose for certain situations.

### Installing STM32CubeMX

> [!important] A third-party account is needed
> You will need a myST account to download and install this tool.

[STM32CubeMX][stm32cubemx] is a tool provided by ST for graphically configuring
STM32 MCUs and MPUs, as well as provide generation of initialization code.

It can be installed by downloading and running the appropriate installer for
your operating system in the `Get Software` section on its web page.

We use STM32CubeMX for configuring pins on our MCU as well as bootstrapping the
initial project. Configuration files for STM32CubeMX have the extension `.ioc`.

[stm32cubemx]: https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubemx.html
